splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA permits plan actuaries to adopt or change actuarial assumptions after the measurement date when calculating an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer plans.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the statute does not require all actuarial assumptions to be locked in by the measurement date, allowing the actuary flexibility to select assumptions after that date.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used in calculating withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date and cannot be changed afterward, providing employers greater predictability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the court-ordered supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as specified in the judgment regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim, in addition to satisfying § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements for successive motions, without the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects the ability to challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide, and raises practical concerns about whether denying pre-election standing would funnel disputes into post-election litigation.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office suffers a cognizable injury from state election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or change election outcomes, sufficient for Article III standing.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged injury from a state's ballot-counting procedures is too speculative or generalized to satisfy Article III's injury-in-fact requirement.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, leading to inconsistent results regarding liability and available remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, which impacts hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for discrimination claims against business operators, allowing broader theories of liability and remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard that limits the scope of actionable discrimination claims and available remedies against business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting the Sentencing Guidelines in criminal cases. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has taken on new significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations, meaning ambiguity in criminal sentencing provisions must be resolved in the defendant's favor rather than deferring to the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative commentary takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or impermissibly expands the guideline text. This affects career offender designations and sentencing ranges for many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson, so conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to rather than interprets the guideline, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under § 3553(f)(1) only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or if possessing any one is disqualifying. This directly determines whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums, affecting liberty interests with disparate outcomes depending on jurisdiction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance to be controlled under federal law, or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. This affects career offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-controlled substance suffices
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is also federally controlled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether revocation of supervised release may be used to punish the defendant for the conduct that violated the conditions, or whether it must serve only the limited purposes of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split on this issue.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying a supervised release violation when revoking supervised release and imposing a new term of imprisonment.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is impermissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must serve the purposes of supervised release rather than punish the defendant for the violating conduct, consistent with the statutory framework distinguishing supervised release from parole.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically prohibit reliance on such changes, while others (and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) allow courts to consider them. This affects prisoners serving lengthy sentences under now-superseded mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement authorizing such consideration is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment, given that the motion arises in a criminal case but concerns a civil fee-shifting matter.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the time limit for appealing a Hyde Amendment fee order follows the civil deadline (60 days under FRAP 4(a)) or the criminal deadline (14 days under FRAP 4(b)). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether appreciation in a debtor's property between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This affects whether Chapter 7 trustees can sell appreciated assets to recover value for creditors after a good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad definition of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation is part of the estate upon conversion, and § 348(f)(1)(A) does not carve it out for the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the Bankruptcy Code's structure and § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors who convert in good faith, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms (but not the fact or duration) of imprisonment must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may bring civil rights claims under Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on the boundary between habeas corpus and civil rights remedies for prisoners challenging conditions or administrative decisions that affect the nature of their confinement but do not directly challenge its fact or duration. The Eighth Circuit highlighted this unresolved conflict in the context of First Step Act earned time credits and BOP transfer decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought as habeas corpus petitions rather than civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights remedies are also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights claims (e.g., Bivens, § 1983, or APA) to challenge conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly implicate the fact or duration of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost without immediate review. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category of orders as meeting the collateral order doctrine's requirements.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the interest can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment or through other procedural mechanisms.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
